housingTypes.question: What types of housing are available to students?
housingTypes.answer: Several options are available to you: Approved or social-purpose university residences: reserved for students, they offer regulated rents, often below market prices. Access is prioritised for students on low incomes (e.g. Crous grant holders). Student service residences: also reserved for students, but with unregulated rents. Standard rental: independent housing rented from a private landlord or through an agency. Homestay or intergenerational housing: a room rented in an occupied home, often at reduced rent.

typologies.question: How do I understand housing types (T1, T2, studio, etc.)?
typologies.answer: Studio: a single living space with a bathroom (bathroom/toilet). T1: a living space + a separate kitchen + bathroom/toilet. T2, T3...: each additional number means one more room (e.g. a T2 has a living room and a bedroom).

chargesIncluded.question: What does "rent including charges" mean?
chargesIncluded.answer: If a listing says "cc" (charges comprises, i.e. charges included), it means that some charges are included in the rent, such as upkeep of shared areas, cold/hot water or electricity. Always check exactly what the charges cover before signing.

header.title: Why create a budget?
header.description: For many people, becoming a student marks the beginning of independence and the need to learn how to plan a budget. Between rent, tuition fees, groceries and outings, it is important to have visibility. A well-prepared budget allows you to:

list.item4: Better plan your projects (travel, driving license, equipment...)
list.item5: Keep peace of mind for your studies
list.item6: Good to know: your higher education institution, as well as the Crous, can support you. Other services (CAF, ADIL, local social services center...) can also help you if needed.

item1.title: 1. Define your monthly resources
item1.description: Start by reviewing your fixed and occasional income. This will help you determine how much you can spend each month.

simulationCard.title: Simulate the amount of your student aid

list.title: Possible resources:
list.item3: Housing aid (APL or ALS via CAF)
list.item8: Student loan guaranteed by the French State

item2.title: 2. Identify your fixed costs
item2.description:
It is important to properly identify the different expenses and have an estimated cost range. Some of these expenses may vary depending on the area, such as rent, transport or food. It is also important to distinguish recurring and mandatory expenses, which generally come back every month, from variable expenses.

Fixed costs are recurring expenses, often unavoidable. They vary depending on your situation (city, accommodation, transport...).

list.title: Examples of fixed costs:
list.item5: Home, health and civil liability insurance

item2.descriptionSubList: These estimates are based on responses from students living away from home and independent students in the OVE 2023 Student Living Conditions survey.

item3.title: 3. Estimate your variable expenses
item3.description: These are expenses that change each month and that you can adjust.

item4.title: 4. Plan for exceptional expenses
item4.description: Even with a good budget, some expenses occur less often but can be costly:

list.item2: Buying a computer or specialized equipment
list.item5: Deposit or agency fees for accommodation

faq.subTitle: Do you have questions? We have answers. This section is designed to provide the most complete and accurate information to help you prepare for student life. We have grouped the most frequently asked questions to make your search easier.

housingTypes.question: What types of housing are available to students?
housingTypes.intro: Several options are available to you:
housingTypes.conventionne: Approved or social-purpose university residences: reserved for students, they offer regulated rents, often below market prices. Access is prioritised for students on low incomes (e.g. Crous grant holders).
housingTypes.conventionneIncludes: Includes: Crous residences, social housing managed directly by social housing bodies (HLM) or by associations.
housingTypes.services: Student service residences, also reserved for students, but with rents that are currently unregulated. In the future, service residences with intermediate rents (between social housing rents and private market rents) will be developed.
housingTypes.classic: Standard rental: independent housing rented from a private landlord or through an agency.
housingTypes.homestay: Homestay or intergenerational housing: a room rented in an occupied home, often at reduced rent.

typologies.question: How do I understand housing types (T1, T2, studio, etc.)?
typologies.studio: Studio: a single living space with a bathroom (bathroom/toilet).
typologies.t1: T1: a living space + a separate kitchen + bathroom/toilet.
typologies.t2t3: T2, T3...: each additional number means one more room (e.g. a T2 has a living room and a bedroom).

chargesIncluded.question: What does “rent including charges” mean?
chargesIncluded.intro: If a listing says "cc" (charges comprises, i.e. charges included), it means that some charges are included in the rent, such as:
chargesIncluded.warning: ⚠️ Always check exactly what the charges cover before signing.
chargesIncluded.legal: Please note: the tenancy agreement and rent receipts must always clearly distinguish the rent amount (which may be regulated for social or intermediate rental housing) from the recoverable rental charges, whose exhaustive list is set by decree. You can find this information at

furnished.question: What is the difference between furnished and unfurnished housing?
furnished.furnished: Furnished: includes a minimum of equipment (bed, hob, fridge, etc.). Rents are generally higher.
furnished.unfurnished: Unfurnished: empty or partly equipped, often with a longer lease (3 years versus 1 year for a furnished home).

energyPerformance.question: What are the DPE and GES ratings? Why do they matter?
energyPerformance.dpe: DPE (energy performance certificate): shows the home's energy consumption (rated from A to G).
energyPerformance.ges: GES (greenhouse gases): measures the emissions linked to the energy used.
energyPerformance.note: 👉 A poorly rated home (E or F: G-rated homes may no longer be rented out since January 2025, except under specific exemptions) may be poorly insulated, expensive to heat and uncomfortable in summer.

whereToFind.question: Where can I find this type of student housing?
whereToFind.answer: Approved university residences and other social housing are listed in the "Find student accommodation" section on monlogementetudiant.beta.gouv.fr

financialAid.cafAids: Personal housing aid from the CAF can help you pay your rent.
financialAid.moreInfo: For more information, you can visit <cafLink></cafLink> and <servicePublicLink></servicePublicLink>

financialAid.simulator: You can check them with our simulator: <link>Simulate my housing aid</link>

guarantor.question: Do I need a guarantor to rent a home?
guarantor.intro: Yes, most landlords require a guarantor: a person (often a parent) who agrees to pay the rent if you cannot. If you don't have one, you can turn to:
guarantor.private: Paid private guarantees: offered by some rental platforms.

documents.question: What documents do I need to put together a rental application?
documents.studentStatus: Proof of student status (certificate of enrolment), only for student housing (university residences, dedicated service residences, not in the private rental market)
documents.rentReceipts: Your last three rent receipts or a certificate of accommodation
documents.contract: Your employment contract or proof of grant, if applicable

crousMobiliteParcoursup.name: Parcoursup mobility aid
crousMobiliteParcoursup.description: Are you in your final year of high school (Terminale), do you have a high school scholarship and do you want to study in another academic district next year? Then you can apply for the Parcoursup mobility aid, worth €500. You can apply from June 2026 via the messervices.etudiant.gouv.fr portal. The aid will be paid in early September, once you are enrolled in higher education.

reasons.terminaleOnly: Reserved for high school students in their final year (Terminale)
reasons.lyceeScholarshipOnly: Reserved for high school scholarship holders
reasons.changingRegion: You must be changing region or academic district next year

crousMobiliteMaster.name: CROUS Master's mobility aid
crousMobiliteMaster.description: Are you completing your bachelor's degree (licence) this year and do you want to enrol in a first-year Master's (Master 1) in another academic region next year? If you hold a CROUS scholarship, you can receive mobility aid of €1,000. You don't need to take any specific steps to apply for the mobility aid. You will need to provide a copy of the following documents: your bachelor's degree certificate and your enrolment certificate for the first year of your Master's (Master 1). Please note: a professional bachelor's degree (licence professionnelle) does not make you eligible for this aid.

reasons.licence3Only: Reserved for students in the 3rd year of their bachelor's degree (licence)
reasons.professionalLicence: A professional bachelor's degree (licence professionnelle) does not make you eligible for this aid
reasons.changingRegion: You must be enrolling in another academic region next year

crousMobiliteMaster.warningProfessionalLicenceUnknown: If your bachelor's degree is a professional one, you will not be eligible for this aid.
